To Boldly Go Insights with Rayfin and GitHub Copilot

→Intelligent UX→Automatic & Governed→Generative UI→Multimodal Insights

Sanjay Narendran
Microsoft · November 2026
Today I want to tell a story about where insights are heading. It has four stages, the four pillars on the right: intelligent UX, where AI-native experiences replace the dashboards people had to read and interpret, then automatic governed insights, then the two combined into Generative UI, and last, the same ideas carried across every kind of data, from the patient record to pathology slides and CT scans. All four run on the same foundation, Microsoft Fabric.

AI-Native User Experiences

What 2026 added to Microsoft Fabric

20252026

Six workloads share one copy of the data, in OneLake.Rayfin brings the user experience, and MCP connects GitHub Copilot and Foundry agents to Fabric.

[Opens on 2025; → or a click on 2026 moves to 2026.] The first pillar opens: intelligent UX, AI-native user experiences. The old way, where a person opens a dashboard, reads it and works out what it means, is giving way to experiences that think with you. Here is the platform that makes it possible. This is Microsoft Fabric as it stood in 2025: six workloads, Copilot in each of them and governance across them, all reading one copy of the data in OneLake, with data from every cloud and system brought in by shortcuts and mirroring, GitHub Copilot as the coding agent in VS Code, and Microsoft Foundry for AI apps and agents. In 2026 two things changed. Rayfin became the user experience: apps with Fabric sign-in, data and hosting, like every app you will see today. And MCP connected the agents to Fabric: GitHub Copilot became the driver of agentic development, building, deploying and querying Fabric for you, and agents built in Microsoft Foundry reach Fabric’s data the same way. Everything in today’s demos was built that way.

The report on the right is written automatically from the semantic model at every refresh, so nobody has to author the executive summary, and it reads top to bottom like a briefing. The same governed data then tells a different story for each persona. [→] The analyst gets the trend detail. [→] The infection-prevention lead gets a view of where to act. How it’s calculatedTry this yourself

Each line is the national pooled Standardized Infection Ratio (SIR): every infection hospitals reported, divided by every infection CDC’s risk models predicted for those same hospitals. Below 1.0 means fewer infections than predicted.

  1. 1
    Source

    CMS Care Compare HAI file, loaded into semantic model CMS, table HAI.

  2. 2
    Query

    One DAX query sums observed and predicted cases per infection, by REPORTYEAR.

  3. 3
    Calculate

    Pooled SIR = Σ observed ÷ Σ predicted. No weighting, filtering or smoothing.

  4. 4
    Draw

    One point per report year. Rounded to 2 decimals only when displayed.

2025 pooled SIR10,805 ÷ 17,570.315 = 0.614958 → 0.61
Change vs 20190.614958 ÷ 0.684675 − 1 = −10.2% → −10%

Why pooled, not an average of hospitals

CMS only publishes a hospital’s SIR when at least one infection is predicted, so many hospitals have no published SIR but are still in the totals. Pooling counts every infection once, which is how NHSN aggregates SIRs for groups of hospitals.

You don’t have to trust this dashboard, the semantic model, or this panel. Here are four independent checks, quickest first.

CLABSICAUTISSI · ColonSSI · HysterectomyMRSAC. diff
1
Recalculate by hand
≈ 1 minute
  • 2025: 10,805 ÷ 17,570.315 = 0.614958 → 0.61, the big number in the panel.
  • Change: 0.614958 ÷ 0.684675 − 1 = −10.2% → −10%, the label under it.
2
Re-run the query in Fabric
≈ 5 minutes
  1. In the Fabric portal, open workspace contoso-quality and semantic model CMS.
  2. Choose Write DAX queries, paste the query below and select Run.
  3. Observed, predicted and hospital counts should match exactly.
DAX · validation query for CLABSICopy
EVALUATE
SUMMARIZECOLUMNS (
    HAI[REPORTYEAR],
    "Observed", SUM ( HAI[HAI_1_NUMERATOR-…: Observed Cases] ),
    "Predicted", SUM ( HAI[HAI_1_ELIGCASES-…: Predicted Cases] ),
    "Pooled SIR", DIVIDE ( SUM ( HAI[…Observed Cases] ), SUM ( HAI[…Predicted Cases] ) )
)
ORDER BY HAI[REPORTYEAR]
3
Trace it back to CMS’s own files
≈ 15 minutes
  1. Download the report year’s snapshot from the CMS hospitals data archive.
  2. Open Healthcare_Associated_Infections-Hospital.csv in Excel.
  3. Observed: =SUMIFS(L:L, I:I, "HAI_1_NUMERATOR")
  4. Predicted: =SUMIFS(L:L, I:I, "HAI_1_ELIGCASES"), then divide.

An automated check repeats this for every infection and year: all 42 infection-years match exactly.

4
Sanity-check against CDC
optional

CDC’s HAI Progress Report publishes national SIRs from the same NHSN system. Expect the same direction and similar size, not identical values.

[Plays through on its own; → skips ahead.] The fourth pillar opens: multimodal insights, where everything so far reaches into clinical data of every kind. It starts with research. A researcher describes a cohort in plain words, adults 50 or older who are former smokers with a lung nodule of at least 6 mm. GitHub Copilot finds the i2b2 terms, fills three panels and runs them on the Cohort Discovery semantic model in Fabric. The count comes back obfuscated, 356 plus or minus 3, so no one can single out a patient. The researcher submits it, and a reviewer approves it in a Rayfin app on Fabric.

[Plays through on its own; → skips ahead.] Patient 360 is a Rayfin app on Fabric that puts one patient’s whole record on one page. This is Ivelisse Nitzsche, a synthetic patient: a lifetime timeline of visits, conditions, her breast cancer and her imaging, read in place from Epic in Snowflake, the PACS and OneLake. Click the slide from her diagnosis and it opens in the app’s own viewer, with an AI map of where the immune cells gather, and we zoom from the whole section into the tumour as it spreads between the fat cells. Click her screening CT and we scroll through a 22 millimetre nodule, see it in three planes, and turn the chest in 3D, from bone to glass lung. These are public research images on a synthetic patient.

Over one breath the tumour moves 2.1 mm, and his lungs change by 843 mL, from 5,106 mL at the start of the cycle to 4,263 mL at 50%.

Radiotherapy teams use this motion to set the margin around the tumour. The CT is from the TCIA 4D-Lung collection, attached to a synthetic patient.

[Plays through on its own; → skips ahead.] The last step brings the conversation back, now about images. In Ask, inside Patient 360, I ask Copilot to play Stephan Rutherford’s 4D CT through one breath, and how far the tumour moves. Copilot finds the patient and opens the scan right in the answer: ten phases of one breath, the lungs as glass, the tumour in orange, airway, heart and spine inside. And the numbers come from the study itself: the tumour moves 2.1 millimetres and the lungs change by 843 millilitres. So the journey runs from a question, to a cohort, to one patient’s record and slides and scans, and back to a conversation.
